name: bag of white rice
descriptions: A plain paper-sack of long-grain white rice, a foundational staple for many cuisines.
Dry, hard individual grains that need cooking to become fluffy and edible.
effects: You pop raw rice into your mouth. The dry, crunchy grains grind between your teeth and quickly turn into uncomfortable abrasives in your mouth.
It leaves a coating of powder on your tongue and throat; oddly filling but thirsty work.

name: all-purpose flour
descriptions: Fine, white flour in a sealed paper bag — the backbone of bread, pastries, and roux.
Raw flour is powdery and pleasant to the nose but is not intended to be eaten uncooked.
effects: You shovel a handful of raw flour into your mouth. It tastes bland and chalky, coats your mouth, and makes you want to cough.
Eating raw flour can cause stomach upset for some people and leaves a dry, gritty feeling.

name: dried spaghetti
descriptions: A long bundle of dried pasta strands, a quick-cooking carb when boiled.
Uncooked it is hard and brittle but lightweight and easy to store.
effects: You bite a raw strand; it snaps with a crisp sound and grinds against your teeth.
It fills the stomach a bit but is very dry and demands water or cooking to be truly palatable.

name: dried kidney beans (500 g)
descriptions: A bag of hard, dried beans common in stews and chilies.
These must be soaked and properly cooked before eating; raw or undercooked kidney beans can cause food poisoning.
effects: You try a spoonful of raw kidney beans. They taste chalky and bitter and quickly make your stomach churn.
Raw kidney beans contain natural toxins that can upset the gut; eating them uncooked often causes nausea and vomiting.

name: rolled oats (500 g)
descriptions: Flattened oat flakes commonly eaten as porridge or muesli.
Often eaten raw mixed with milk or yogurt, or cooked into warm cereal.
effects: You chew raw oats; they are pleasantly nutty and slightly chewy, leaving a hearty, grainy texture.
They are filling and comforting even without cooking, though they benefit from soaking or milk.

name: granulated sugar (500 g)
descriptions: A bag of fine white sugar, used to sweeten beverages and baked goods.
Eating sugar straight gives a sharp sweet hit but lacks substance.
effects: You pour a spoon of dry sugar into your mouth. It's intensely sweet and dissolves quickly, giving a quick jolt.
The sugar leaves a sticky film and provides a burst of quick energy but little lasting satisfaction.

name: table salt (200 g)
descriptions: Fine iodized salt in a small shaker or packet — essential for seasoning.
Eating salt by itself is unpleasant and promotes dehydration.
effects: You lick a pinch of salt. It scorches the tongue and makes your mouth water, then leaves you parched.
A mouthful of salt can make you feel dizzy and thirsty; it's not satisfying as a food on its own.

name: vegetable cooking oil
descriptions: A clear bottle of neutral vegetable oil used for frying and dressings.
High-calorie liquid fat; safe to consume in small quantities but heavy and slick when eaten plain.
effects: You swallow a mouthful of oil. It's slick and fills the mouth with a fatty coating, leaving a heavy, greasy sensation.
Oil provides a lot of calories quickly but feels greasy and can make you nauseous if taken in large amounts.

name: canned tomatoes (400 g can)
descriptions: A tin of stewed tomatoes — ready to add to sauces, soups, and stews.
Soft, acidic, and already cooked; safe and hydrating to eat straight from the can.
effects: You eat spoonfuls of canned tomatoes. They're tangy, juicy, and relieve thirst a little while providing a pleasant acidic bite.
The tomato juices are refreshing and comforting in a simple, cooked way.

name: dried red lentils
descriptions: Small, lens-shaped legumes that cook relatively quickly into soups and dals.
Like most dried pulses, they are intended to be soaked or boiled before eating.
effects: You crunch down on raw lentils; they are hard and mildly bitter, and your stomach protests after a few mouthfuls.
Undercooked or raw lentils can cause bloating and mild digestive discomfort for some people.

name: raw potatoes (bag, 2 kg)
descriptions: A burlap sack of raw potatoes — versatile when cooked into mash, roast, or fries.
Raw potato flesh is starchy and crunchy, with a slightly bitter edge if green or sprouted.
effects: You bite into a raw potato. It's starchy and crunchy, with an unappealing dry texture and a hint of bitterness.
A few bites are filling but the taste is bland compared to when potatoes are cooked.

name: Bag of white rice (uncooked)
descriptions: A common staple grain: long-grain white rice in a simple paper sack.
Used worldwide as a base for many meals; sold here in its uncooked, dry form.
Edible raw in small amounts but very dry and hard; normally requires boiling to be palatable.
effects: You shovel a handful of hard, uncooked grains into your mouth. They crackle and grind between your teeth, offering a plain, starchy bite.
The rice feels filling but gritty; it leaves your mouth and throat dry and makes you reach for water.

name: Wheat flour (bag)
descriptions: A sack of milled wheat flour — the basis for bread, pasta, and countless baked staples.
Sold raw and dusty; each mouthful is powdery and bland unless mixed or cooked.
effects: You scoop a spoonful of raw flour and swallow. The powder clings to your mouth and throat, leaving a chalky, unpleasant texture.
Flour swells and absorbs moisture in your mouth, so while it briefly fills you, it makes you thirsty and a little queasy if you eat a lot.

name: Cornmeal (maize flour)
descriptions: Ground dried maize used for staples like porridge, flatbreads, and polenta.
Dry and granular when uncooked; nutritious once prepared with water or heat.
effects: You eat a mouthful of raw cornmeal; it has a slightly coarse, grainy texture and a bland corn taste.
It gives a modest sense of fullness but makes your mouth feel dry and sandy.

name: Dried mixed beans
descriptions: A pouch of assorted dried beans (kidney, navy, black), a protein-rich staple in many cuisines.
Sold uncooked and hard; normally soaked and boiled before eating.
effects: You chew a few raw beans. They are very firm and starchy with an earthy flavor; they crunch and then soften slightly.
They provide a genuine sense of bulkiness in your stomach but are unpleasantly dry and grainy eaten without cooking.

name: Dried lentils
descriptions: Small, shelf-stable legumes valued across many cultures for protein and fiber.
They cook quickly compared with many beans but are sold here in raw, uncooked form.
effects: A mouthful of raw lentils is small and starchy, with a faint nuttiness. They crunch at first and then chew into a gritty paste.
They fill you more than you'd expect for their size, though they leave you a bit dry.

name: Uncooked dried pasta
descriptions: Strips or shapes of dried wheat pasta — a global carbohydrate staple when boiled.
Brittle and hard while uncooked; commonly stored for long periods.
effects: You bite into a piece of dry pasta; it snaps and crunches, then grinds into a dry, floury paste.
It is surprisingly filling but very dehydrating and can be uncomfortable to chew in quantity.

name: Granulated sugar
descriptions: Refined white sugar in a small packet — used worldwide to sweeten foods and beverages.
Highly caloric but offers little lasting fullness; very sweet when eaten straight.
effects: You dump a spoonful of dry sugar into your mouth. It dissolves instantly, a rush of sweetness that perks you up briefly.
The quick sugar spike gives immediate energy but barely fills you and leaves you wanting water.

name: Table salt (packet)
descriptions: A small sachet of refined salt, essential for seasoning and preservation worldwide.
Eating it straight is harsh and rapidly dehydrating.
effects: You tip a pinch of pure salt into your mouth. The immediate sting of sodium overwhelms your taste buds and dries your throat.
Salt gives no real nourishment and makes you very thirsty; too much leaves you drained.

name: Canned tomatoes (sealed can)
descriptions: A can of preserved tomatoes — common for sauces and stews around the globe.
Usually ready-to-eat when drained; tangy, watery, and slightly acidic.
effects: You spoon some canned tomatoes straight from the can. They are soft, juicy, and tangy — fairly refreshing eaten as-is.
Their water content helps quench thirst a bit and they offer a pleasant, acidic bite.

name: Dried Black Beans (500 g)
descriptions: A pouch of dried black beans — staple legume meant for soaking and long simmering.
Eating them raw is chalky and tough; they’re meant to be cooked to soften and unlock flavor.
effects: You crunch on a few raw beans; they’re hard and bitter with a dusty aftertaste.
They take up space in your stomach and quiet your appetite for a while, though they lack the comfort of a cooked meal.

name: Raw Potatoes (3 pcs)
descriptions: A small bundle of raw white potatoes, unpeeled.
Firm and starchy; raw potato flesh is crunchy and slightly bitter compared to boiled or roasted.
effects: You bite into a raw potato; the flesh is crisp, starchy, and a touch astringent.
It fills you with a blunt, dense satiation but lacks the mellow comfort of cooked potato.

name: Raw Carrots (bunch)
descriptions: A small bunch of fresh raw carrots with green tops trimmed.
Crisp, sweet, and perfectly edible raw — a portable, healthy snack.
effects: You snap off a carrot and bite into it; it’s juicy and sweet with a satisfying crunch.
The fresh vegetal flavor refreshes your mouth and makes you feel slightly more alert.

name: Raw Tomatoes (3 pcs)
descriptions: Three vine-ripened tomatoes, unprepared.
Juicy and acidic; perfectly fine to eat raw and refreshing.
effects: You bite into a tomato and a burst of sweet-tart juice floods your mouth.
The acidity wakes you up and leaves a clean, refreshing feeling.

name: Carton of Raw Eggs
descriptions: A dozen uncooked eggs in a cardboard carton.
Intended for cooking; eating raw eggs is unpalatable and carries a risk of foodborne illness.
effects: You crack and swallow a raw egg; the slimy texture and metallic edge make you gag.
The flavor is dull and unsettling, and the experience leaves you queasy rather than nourished.

name: Whole Raw Chicken (uncooked)
descriptions: A whole raw chicken, uncleaned and unprepared.
Raw poultry is unsafe to eat as-is and can cause severe foodborne sickness.
effects: You attempt to bite into raw chicken; the texture is slimy and the smell is faintly sour.
The meat leaves a lingering nausea and a heavy sense of illness rather than any real nourishment.

name: Fresh tomatoes (3 pieces)
descriptions: Three ripe tomatoes, firm and glossy with a sweet-tart aroma.
Juicy and ready to eat raw or to add to salads and sauces.
effects: You bite into a tomato and juice bursts across your tongue — sweet, tangy and refreshing.
The flesh is hydrating and light, leaving a clean, fresh taste.

name: Russet potatoes (4 count)
descriptions: A small bag with four russet potatoes; starchy and versatile when cooked.
Raw potatoes are firm, mildly earthy, and a little bitter if eaten uncooked.
effects: You gnaw on a raw potato: it's starchy and slightly chalky, filling you up though not very palatable.
The raw flesh leaves an earthy aftertaste but provides bulk.

name: Tomato seed packet (20 seeds)
descriptions: A small envelope containing about 20 tomato seeds for planting.
Not meant for eating; intended for sowing in a garden or pot.

name: Raw beef steak (250 g)
descriptions: A 250 g cut of raw beef steak, bright red with some marbling.
Intended to be cooked; eating raw red meat can cause digestive upset and risk of pathogens.
effects: You take a bite of the uncooked steak; the texture is chewy and metallic, and it leaves a heavy, oily feeling.
Raw red meat can sit poorly in the stomach and may leave you queasy and weak.

name: Raw ground beef
descriptions: A 500 g pack of raw minced beef — convenient for many recipes but riskier eaten uncooked.
Ground meat has more exposed surface area and a higher chance of carrying harmful bacteria.
effects: You taste the raw minced beef; the soft, pasty texture and iron-rich flavor make your stomach churn.
Eating raw ground beef is likely to cause severe gastrointestinal distress and possible foodborne illness.

name: Whole raw chicken (approx. 1.5 kg)
descriptions: A whole raw chicken, plucked and gutted, ready to be cooked.
Raw poultry is especially dangerous to consume due to high risk of salmonella and campylobacter.
effects: You attempt to eat raw chicken; the slimy texture and strong raw smell churn your stomach and make you feel faint.
Consuming raw poultry is highly likely to trigger severe food poisoning and immediate weakness.

name: canned tuna (in oil)
descriptions: A sealed tin of ready-to-eat tuna preserved in oil.
Shelf-stable, savory and oily — meant to be eaten straight from the can or used in recipes.
effects: You eat spoonfuls of oily tuna straight from the can — salty, fishy and filling.
It sits well in the stomach and gives a sustained savory energy boost.

name: smoked salmon (vacuum-packed)
descriptions: A thinly sliced pack of smoked salmon that is ready-to-eat.
Rich, smokey fish cured for preservation and flavor.
effects: You eat a slice of smoked salmon as-is; it's oily, smoky and intensely savory.
The rich fats make it feel satisfying and give a heavy energy lift.

name: raw salmon filet (fresh)
descriptions: A fresh, uncooked salmon filet on ice.
Commonly used for cooking or sushi when properly handled, but raw on its own can be risky.
effects: You bite into the raw salmon—slimy, cold and metallic. The taste and texture are off-putting if not prepared properly.
Eating it raw like this makes your stomach churn and can make you feel very unwell.

name: raw shrimp (peeled, fresh)
descriptions: A small tray of fresh, uncooked peeled shrimp.
Shrimp are normally cooked; raw shrimp can carry pathogens if not sushi-grade and handled correctly.
effects: You pop a raw shrimp into your mouth; it is chewy, slippery and has an unpleasant briny raw taste.
It quickly makes your stomach turn and can lead to severe nausea and weakness.

name: frozen cooked shrimp (thawed)
descriptions: A packet of pre-cooked shrimp that has been frozen and then thawed for use.
Safe to eat cold or heated, convenient seafood protein.
effects: You eat a thawed cooked shrimp; it's tender, slightly sweet and pleasantly briny.
It satisfies hunger with a light seafood flavor and doesn't upset your stomach.

name: fresh apple
descriptions: A crisp red apple, freshly picked.
Juicy and sweet, ready to eat with no preparation.
effects: You bite the apple and enjoy a crisp, juicy crunch. It refreshes your mouth and quenches a bit of thirst.
The taste is sweet and satisfying and leaves you feeling a little more energized.

name: head of lettuce
descriptions: A fresh head of green lettuce, crisp leaves ideal for salads.
Mild and watery, typically eaten raw as part of meals.
effects: You eat a few raw leaves; they are cool, watery, and faintly bitter.
They don't fill you much but refresh and add a light hydration boost.

name: tomato seed packet
descriptions: A small paper packet containing tomato seeds for planting.
Designed for sowing into soil to grow tomato plants.
effects: You look at the tiny seeds, imagining ripe tomatoes later — not meant for eating raw straight from the packet.

name: bottle of olive oil (500 ml)
descriptions: A half-liter bottle of extra-virgin olive oil.
Used for cooking, dressings or adding fat and flavor — oily and dense when consumed straight.
effects: You swallow a tablespoon of olive oil. The oily mouthfeel coats your throat and leaves you slightly queasy.
It provides a concentrated caloric hit but makes you feel dehydrated and heavy.

name: loaf of bread (whole)
descriptions: A freshly baked whole loaf of bread, crusty outside and soft inside.
A staple carbohydrate, meant to be sliced and eaten.
effects: You tear off a thick slice and eat it plain; the warm crumb is satisfying and filling.
It provides steady fullness and a moderate energy lift.

name: dried seaweed snack (pack)
descriptions: A small pack of roasted, salted seaweed sheets.
Light, crisp and intensely salty, often eaten as a snack or garnish.
effects: You eat a sheet of dried seaweed; it's thin, crunchy and overtly salty.
It satisfies a light craving but leaves you a touch thirsty from the salt.

name: 10 kg Bag of White Rice
descriptions: A large sack of milled white rice — clean, dry grains commonly used as a staple carbohydrate.
Packed for storage; edible as-is but very dry and crunchy when eaten without cooking.
effects: You shovel a handful of raw rice into your mouth; the grains are hard and extremely dry, crunching loudly.
The rice gives a steady, filling sensation but leaves your mouth dry and in need of water.

name: 500 g Pack of Dry Pasta
descriptions: Standard durum-wheat pasta in a sealed bag — designed to be boiled before eating.
Firm, brittle strands or shapes that will soften only after cooking.
effects: You crunch a piece of raw pasta; it tastes bland and starchy with a brittle snap.
It provides some quick carbohydrate satisfaction but is more pleasant when cooked.

name: Canned Mixed Beans (400 g)
descriptions: A ready-to-eat can of mixed beans in light brine — protein-rich and shelf-stable.
Can be eaten straight from the can although many prefer to heat and season them first.
effects: You eat beans directly from the can; they are soft, slightly salty, and filling.
They settle pleasantly in your stomach and give a lasting fullness and energy boost.

name: Loaf of Whole Wheat Bread
descriptions: A freshly baked whole wheat loaf, pre-sliced and wrapped.
Soft crumb with a hearty flavor — commonly used for sandwiches and toast.
effects: You tear off a slice and eat it plain; the bread is filling and slightly moist.
The whole grains leave a wholesome, satisfying aftertaste.

name: Bag of Fresh Apples (4)
descriptions: A small bag containing four crisp apples — firm, juicy, and ready to eat.
Great raw snack with natural sugars and hydration.
effects: You bite into an apple, the juice popping and the flesh sweet-tart and refreshing.
The fruit instantly cools and quenches the mouth while giving a pleasant energy lift.

name: Bunch of Bananas (5)
descriptions: Five ripe bananas joined at the stem — soft, sweet, and high in potassium.
Peel and eat raw for a quick, portable snack.
effects: You peel a banana and eat it; the texture is creamy and sweet with an immediate energy lift.
Bananas are easy on the stomach and fill you quickly.

name: Bunch of Carrots
descriptions: A tied bunch of fresh carrots with firm, orange roots and leafy tops.
Crunchy and sweet, excellent raw as a snack or for cooking.
effects: You snap a carrot and eat it raw; the crisp texture and sweet earthiness brighten the palate.
Carrots are satisfying and lightly hydrating with a gentle energy boost.

name: Fresh Tomatoes (4)
descriptions: Four ripe tomatoes, juicy and slightly acidic, good for salads or eating raw.
Soft skin and pulpy interior full of flavor and moisture.
effects: You bite a tomato and juice runs down your chin; the flavor is sweet-tart and very refreshing.
Tomatoes hydrate and brighten your senses while filling you a little.

name: Bag of Potatoes (3 kg)
descriptions: A heavy bag containing starchy potatoes — versatile for boiling, baking, or frying.
Raw they are firm and bland; normally cooked before eating.
effects: You bite into a raw potato: it's firm, slightly grainy, and very bland — more satisfying when cooked.
Raw potato offers substantial bulk and a slow-release carbohydrate feeling.

name: Bottle of Olive Oil (250 ml)
descriptions: A small bottle of cold-pressed olive oil — rich in fats and calories, commonly used as a dressing or cooking oil.
High in energy density; consuming it neat is oily and heavy.
effects: You take a spoonful of olive oil; it slicks your mouth and throat with a fatty, fruity coat.
The oil provides a strong caloric surge and leaves a lingering, greasy sensation.

name: Jar of Table Salt (150 g)
descriptions: A small jar of fine table salt — essential seasoning but intense and drying when eaten alone.
Used sparingly for flavor; direct consumption can be unpleasant.
effects: You lick a spoonful of salt; the immediate metallic, saline sting makes your mouth pucker and your throat feel dry.
Salt eaten on its own leaves you thirsty and slightly unsettled.

name: Bag of Brown Sugar (500 g)
descriptions: A sealed bag of moist brown sugar — sweet, caramel-tinged granules used in baking and sweetening.
Eating raw sugar is straightforward but very sweet.
effects: You eat a spoonful of brown sugar; it's intensely sweet with a molasses undertone and quickly spikes your energy.
The sugar leaves a lingering sweetness and a quick energy rush.

name: Strawberry Seed Packet
descriptions: A small envelope of strawberry seeds intended for planting in a garden or pot.
Tiny seeds that are edible but extremely small and not particularly filling.
effects: You pop a few strawberry seeds into your mouth; they are minute and mostly tasteless, with a slightly gritty texture.
Eating them raw does little beyond a faint plantlike note and a tiny sense of fullness.

name: Tomato Seed Packet
descriptions: A small packet of tomato seeds for home gardening.
Like other seeds, they are edible in tiny amounts but mainly meant for planting.
effects: You chew a few tomato seeds; they are tiny, slightly bitter, and offer negligible sustenance.
They leave a faint tomato-like note but are not satisfying on their own.

name: Head of Lettuce
descriptions: A crisp head of leafy lettuce — cool, mild, and perfect for salads or raw sandwiches.
Very hydrating and light in calories.
effects: You tear off a leaf and eat it; the lettuce is cool, crisp, and refreshing.
It quenches your thirst slightly and gives a light, clean sensation.

name: Raw Garlic Bulb (single)
descriptions: A whole head of garlic with several cloves; raw, pungent, and concentrated.
Commonly used as seasoning; eating raw cloves is intense and sharp.
effects: You bite into a raw clove; the flavor is fiery, sulfurous, and may make your eyes water.
Garlic eaten raw can be invigorating but leaves a strong aftertaste and breath.

name: bag of long-grain rice (1 kg)
descriptions: A 1 kg paper sack of dry long-grain white rice — staple, neutral-smelling and shelf-stable.
Uncooked grains are hard and brittle; convenient for bulk storage and long meals.
effects: You crunch through hard, dry grains — starchy, bland and oddly filling. Eating rice dry leaves a gritty mouthfeel and a strong thirst.
Comforting in quantity but noticeably drying without any liquid.

name: dried spaghetti pasta (500 g)
descriptions: A 500 g bundle of dried durum wheat spaghetti — brittle, long strands bundled in a pack.
Pasta stores well and cooks into a filling base for many meals.
effects: The raw strands snap and crunch; tasting them dry gives a starchy, slightly sweet bite that fills quickly but leaves the mouth parched.
Not pleasant raw, but undeniably filling.

name: all-purpose flour (1 kg)
descriptions: A 1 kg bag of sifted all-purpose wheat flour — soft, powdery and highly versatile for baking and thickening.
Raw flour is shelf-stable but gritty and clumping when eaten straight.
effects: A mouthful of raw flour feels chalky and dry, clinging to the tongue and teeth. It settles the stomach but is bland and slightly uncomfortable.
Not dangerous in small amounts but unpleasant to eat on its own.

name: table salt (250 g)
descriptions: A small container of fine-grain table salt — essential seasoning and a powerful flavor concentrate.
Very shelf-stable; strong taste means small amounts are typical.
effects: A pinch becomes a sharp, almost painful salt bite; a spoonful is intensely bracing and makes your mouth and throat dry and very thirsty.
Salt eaten straight quickly makes you crave water.

name: vegetable cooking oil (1 L)
descriptions: A one-litre bottle of neutral vegetable oil — useful for frying, baking and dressing.
High-calorie, shelf-stable liquid with a smooth, oily mouthfeel.
effects: Swallowing a spoonful of oil yields a slick, heavy coating in the mouth and throat; it's calorically dense and leaves a greasy aftertaste.
Provides sustained energy but feels heavy and can make you feel oily.

name: canned crushed tomatoes (400 g)
descriptions: A 400 g tin of cooked crushed tomatoes in their juices — tangy and ready to use as a sauce base.
Convenient conserve that adds moisture, acidity and tomato flavor to dishes.
effects: Spoonfuls of soft, saucy tomatoes are tangy and slightly sweet; they are easy to eat straight from the can and refresh the mouth.
Provides a welcome moistness compared to dry staples.

name: canned mixed beans (400 g)
descriptions: A 400 g can of mixed cooked beans in brine — protein-rich, starchy and ready-to-eat.
Hearty conserve that is filling and stores long on the shelf.
effects: The soft beans are savory and satisfying straight from the can, with a starchy bite and noticeable saltiness from the brine.
Filling and comfortingly substantial.

name: jar of fruit jam (strawberry, 340 g)
descriptions: A 340 g jar of strawberry jam — thick, sweet fruit preserve made from fruit and sugar.
Used as a spread or sweetener; sticky and highly caloric.
effects: A spoonful of jam is intensely sweet and fruity, clinging to the tongue in a thick, sticky coat.
Pleasant and comforting, but sugary and quickly filling.

name: canned tuna in water (185 g)
descriptions: A 185 g can of cooked, drained tuna preserved in water — flaky, salty and protein-dense.
Ready-to-eat, useful for sandwiches, salads or straight from the can.
effects: Flaky, savory fish with a slightly metallic, fishy tang; satisfying and protein-rich when eaten right out of the can.
Substantial and restoring without preparation.

name: dried lentils (500 g)
descriptions: A 500 g bag of small dried lentils — quick-cooking legumes high in protein and fiber.
Dry and hard when uncooked; a staple for stews and bulk meals.
effects: Crunchy and earthy when eaten raw; they fill the belly but are dry and a bit gritty without cooking.
Nutty flavor but thirst-inducing.

name: instant coffee granules (100 g)
descriptions: A small jar of instant coffee granules — concentrated, dehydrated coffee for quick brewing.
Strong aroma; typically dissolved in hot water rather than eaten dry.
effects: Chewing dry coffee granules produces a bitter, astringent taste and a dry scratchy feeling; a jittery caffeine edge can come through after swallowing.
Unpleasant on its own but stimulating.

name: bouillon cubes (beef, pack of 6)
descriptions: A small wrapped pack of concentrated bouillon cubes — intensely seasoned and salty, meant for dissolving.
Convenient for adding umami to soups and stews.
effects: Chewing a bouillon cube gives an overpowering salty, savory blast that can make your mouth water then go dry; very concentrated flavor.
Hard to eat straight and thirst-inducing due to high salt and seasoning.

name: jar of honey (500 g)
descriptions: A 500 g jar of raw honey — viscous, sweet and shelf-stable natural sweetener.
Sticky and dense, keeps well and can be used for sweetening or as a fast energy source.
effects: A spoonful of thick honey coats the mouth in warm sweetness, soothing and intensely caloric; it lingers long on the tongue.
Comforting energy boost with a heavy mouthfeel.

name: powdered milk (500 g)
descriptions: A 500 g box of dried whole milk powder — shelf-stable dairy substitute that reconstitutes with water.
Dry and slightly sweet when eaten alone; commonly used in baking or rehydrated for drinking.
effects: Dry milk powder tastes chalky and clumpy; a faint dairy sweetness is present, but it is much more palatable when mixed with liquid.
Slightly filling but a little drying when consumed as-is.

name: Vinegar (250 ml)
descriptions: A 250 ml bottle of white vinegar — acidic, sharp and shelf-stable.
Used for cooking, cleaning and preserving; sour and pungent.
effects: You chug down the vinegar, the sour liquid burning your throat and making your eyes water.
Unpleasant on its own but useful for seasoning or preserving.
You feel nauseous and sick.
